title: "Why Enzyme and not JAX?"
subtitle: "Differentiating programs whose efficient form is irregular"
---

"Why do you use Julia instead of JAX?" is a fair question, and "JAX can't sort" is the
wrong answer: `jax.lax.sort` is differentiable. The real difference is the
**execution model**.

JAX differentiates *pure functions over fixed-shape arrays with a static computation
graph*. Anything that fits that model runs well, often better than hand-written code,
because XLA fuses and vectorises it. [Enzyme](https://enzyme.mit.edu) differentiates
*the imperative program as written*, including in-place mutation, data-dependent loop
bounds and growing buffers. When an algorithm's efficient form is **irregular**, JAX
makes you regularise it with padding, masks, static trip counts or implicit
differentiation. Enzyme lets you keep it.

Each example below implements the same loss three times, with Enzyme.jl, with
[Reactant.jl](https://github.com/EnzymeAD/Reactant.jl), and with JAX, checks that all
three give the same gradient, and times them on a CUDA GPU. Reactant is the control: it
is Julia compiled through XLA, the same static-graph model as JAX. Where Reactant hits
the same wall as JAX, the cause is the execution model, not the language.

## Where the gap shows up

**Data-dependent output size or sparsity**
: Compaction and filtering (`x[mask]`, `push!`), sparse assembly with data-dependent
  fill-in, contact detection, tree codes (octrees, Barnes–Hut). JAX needs a static upper
  bound and masks.

**Data-dependent control flow**
: Iterative solvers with convergence tests, adaptive time stepping. JAX cannot
  reverse-differentiate `lax.while_loop`, so you fix the iteration count or switch to
  implicit differentiation.

**Sequential in-place updates**
: Gauss–Seidel, SOR, Thomas algorithm, sweeps where element *i* depends on the
  just-updated *i−1*. In JAX these become `lax.scan` with the whole array as carry, and
  reverse mode stores every carry unless you rematerialise.

**Irregular neighbour access**
: Particle methods with cell lists (sort by cell, loop over a data-dependent number of
  neighbours), scatter-accumulate with data-dependent indices, histogramming, resampling.

## Where JAX wins

Dense, batched, regular work: most of machine learning, many PDE stencils, anything
whose naive cost already equals its smart cost. There the regularised JAX version is
often faster despite padding, because XLA fuses and the hardware wants regular access.
And the advantage on this site is **Enzyme's**, not Julia's: Julia AD tools that do not
support mutation (Zygote) cannot do this either.
